data.title: Valid Palindrome
data.summary:
Input: A string s.
Output: A boolean indicating whether the string is a palindrome after converting all uppercase letters into lowercase letters and removing all non-alphanumeric characters.
Rules: Empty strings read as palindromes.

import random
def generate(rng, n):
    chars = [chr(rng.randint(32, 126)) for _ in range(n)]
    return ["".join(chars)]

def generate_worst(rng, n):
    half = [chr(rng.randint(97, 122)) for _ in range(n // 2)]
    return ["".join(half + half[::-1])]

data.key_insight: We can check if the string is a palindrome efficiently by maintaining two pointers, one starting at the beginning and the other at the end, moving them inward while skipping any non-alphanumeric characters.

steps.title: Initialize pointers
steps.detail: Set up a left pointer at index 0 and a right pointer at the last index of the string.

steps.title: Traverse and compare
steps.detail: While the left pointer is less than the right pointer, skip non-alphanumeric characters on both sides and compare the lowercase versions of the characters at both pointers.

steps.title: Return result
steps.detail: If any mismatch is found, return false. If the pointers cross without mismatch, return true.

data.pattern_summary: Use two indices moving towards each other from opposite ends of a sequence to compare or process elements in place without extra collection overhead.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. We can check symmetry by starting at both ends and moving inward.

pattern_options.name: Hash map lookup
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. We need to check sequence order and symmetry, not frequency counts.

pattern_options.name: Sliding window
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. A sliding window tracks contiguous subsegments of a specific size or condition, not overall sequence symmetry.

pattern_options.name: Dynamic programming
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. The problem does not require finding optimal subproblems or overlapping states.

signals.phrase: indicating whether the string is a palindrome
signals.hint: Palindromes require matching characters from the outside in.

signals.phrase: after converting all uppercase letters into lowercase letters and removing all non-alphanumeric characters

data.brute_force_idea: First, iterate through the string to build a new list of filtered alphanumeric lowercase characters. Then, use nested loops to compare every pair of indices to check if characters equidistant from the ends match.
data.brute_force_why: The outer loop runs n times and the inner loop runs n times for each outer iteration, resulting in n squared comparisons.
data.bottleneck: Using a nested loop to check symmetry is redundant because a single index advancement from each end can verify the condition in linear time.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how many loops are used to check the symmetry of the filtered list.
Do you need to check every combination of i and j, or do corresponding positions have a fixed relationship?
Notice that the inner loop searches for the matching index instead of directly calculating it.

data.overview: The algorithm uses two pointers starting at opposite ends of the string and moving inward. It skips non-alphanumeric characters and compares the lowercase versions of the characters until they meet or mismatch.
data.intuition: Imagine two people standing at opposite ends of a long word written on the floor, walking towards the center while ignoring punctuation and spaces, checking if they step on matching letters.

pitfalls: Forgetting to check left < right inside the inner loops when skipping characters, which can cause pointers to cross.
Not handling case sensitivity correctly by omitting the lower() method.
Failing to account for strings with only non-alphanumeric characters.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The brute force solution wastes time creating a new filtered string and uses nested loops to compare characters, leading to quadratic time complexity. The optimized two-pointer approach removes this bottleneck by evaluating characters in place from both ends toward the center, skipping non-alphanumeric characters without allocating extra memory.

derivation.note: The while loop runs proportional to the input size n as pointers move inward.
Inner while loops skip non-alphanumeric characters, collectively scanning each character at most once.
Performs a constant-time lowercase conversion and comparison for each valid pair.

data.time_summary: Lines 5 through 13 constitute a single pass over the string. The measured evidence confirms that when n doubles from 16 to 32, the step count increases from 52 to 100 (approximately doubling), verifying O(n) linear time complexity.
data.space_summary: Only two integer pointers (left and right) are stored, meaning no additional data structures scale with the input. This results in O(1) constant space complexity.
data.takeaway: When checking symmetry or properties across a sequential structure like a string or array, use converging two pointers to avoid allocating extra memory and scanning elements more than once.
mistakes: Forgetting to increment the left pointer or decrement the right pointer after a mismatch check, which results in an infinite loop.
Failing to handle edge cases like strings with no alphanumeric characters, where left and right pointers cross without stopping.
Using nested loops to compare elements as done in the brute force approach, which needlessly increases time complexity to O(n^2).
